criteria.descriptor: Full marks: every technical claim is correct — post-filtering truncates results and cannot be fixed by a fixed over-fetch; the pre-filter predicate (tenant/public/group/user with must/should) is well-formed; the filtered-HNSW recall problem and Qdrant's payload-index + full_scan_threshold mitigation are stated accurately; and the query-time group-resolution vs denormalization mechanics (set_payload, no re-embedding on ACL edits) are right. Deduct for invented mechanisms, claiming metadata filters are always exact/free, or asserting membership changes require re-embedding.

Full marks: covers the core diagnosis (correctness AND security) plus all four required dimensions (a) ACL modeling + pushed pre-filter, (b) filtered-ANN recall/perf mitigation, (c) membership-change consistency, and (d) a residual channel with mitigation. Deduct proportionally for each dimension omitted or left superficial.

Full marks: justifies WHY pre-filtering beats post-filtering (ANN ranks the whole space) rather than merely asserting it, and weighs at least one real trade-off (denormalized ACLs vs query-time resolution, or filter selectivity vs recall/latency) with the consequences of each choice. Partial credit for correct choices stated without mechanism-level justification.

Full marks: a well-organized review that separates the diagnosis from the redesign, uses correct vocabulary (pre- vs post-filter, payload/ACL, HNSW recall, tenant isolation) precisely, and is unambiguous about which layer enforces the invariant. Deduct for disorganized, vague, or jargon-name-dropping answers.

expected_answer_points: Diagnoses the correctness failure of post-filtering: because ANN scores over all vectors, the top-k window is chosen before permissions apply, so authorized-but-lower-ranked chunks are never retrieved and the result set silently shrinks below k, with no fixed over-fetch factor able to guarantee completeness.

Diagnoses the security failure: fetching unauthorized content into the process risks leakage to the LLM/citations/logs and via side channels (filtered counts, latency), and stresses that enforcement must live at the retrieval layer, not be delegated to the LLM through prompt instructions.

Prescribes modeling ACLs in the payload (tenant_id, visibility, allowed_group_ids/allowed_user_ids) with payload indexes, and pushing a hard permission predicate into the vector search as a pre-filter (must tenant + should public/group-intersection/user-match) so ANN only ranks authorized candidates.

Explains that pre-filtering an HNSW index can degrade recall and that Qdrant mitigates it via payload-indexed filterable HNSW plus a full_scan_threshold that falls back to exact search on small filtered subsets — i.e. filters are not free and require indexing/tuning.

Handles membership-change consistency by storing slowly-changing group ids on documents and resolving user->groups at query time (so revocations apply immediately without re-indexing), instead of denormalizing user lists into every chunk (write amplification / stale grants); notes ACL edits are a cheap set_payload with no re-embedding, and bounds any membership cache with a short TTL.

Identifies a concrete residual leakage channel after correct filtering (e.g. a cache keyed only on query text serving one principal's results to another, or the revocation staleness window) and gives a specific mitigation (key caches by principal/permission-set, defense-in-depth ACL re-check at citation/generation time).

Surfaces at least one explicit trade-off, e.g. denormalized user lists (fast queries, painful revocation) vs query-time group resolution (immediate revocation, extra query-time lookup), or filter selectivity vs recall/latency.
common_pitfalls: Proposes 'just over-fetch a much larger k, then filter' as the fix without recognizing it is unbounded — an authorized chunk can sit arbitrarily deep, so no fixed multiplier guarantees a complete result set; only pushing the predicate into the search does.

Treats access control as a prompt problem, e.g. instructing the LLM to 'only use documents the user is allowed to see' or to ignore restricted content, instead of enforcing it as a hard retrieval-layer filter.

Denormalizes full allowed-user lists into every chunk payload and misses the write-amplification / stale-grant fallout when membership changes, or wrongly claims a group change requires re-embedding the affected chunks.

Ignores the filtered-ANN recall interaction entirely — assumes a metadata filter is exact and cost-free, unaware that HNSW traversal over a filtered subset needs payload indexes and a full-scan fallback to stay correct.
Conflates relevance metadata filtering (date, source, language as soft ranking signals) with security filtering, applying ACLs as a re-ranking boost rather than a mandatory must-pass predicate.

Stops at 'add a filter' and never addresses residual channels — shared query-keyed caches, source/citation display, or count/latency side channels — so a technically correct filter still leaks across principals.
reference_answer:
Diagnosis. Retrieve-then-drop is broken on two axes. Correctness: the ANN search is scored over ALL vectors, so the top-10 window is chosen without regard to permissions. For a restricted user, highly relevant chunks they ARE allowed to see may sit at rank 50 or 5000, while the top-10 fills up with public/other-tenant chunks that then get dropped in app code. The user is left with a silently truncated set (often far fewer than 10) and degraded or empty answers, and there is no fixed over-fetch factor that fixes this because an authorized chunk can be arbitrarily deep. Security: any unauthorized content that is fetched is now inside the process and one bug away from reaching the LLM, the citations, or logs; and observable side channels (how many results were filtered, latency, 'no answer') leak the existence of restricted material. Access control must be a retrieval-layer invariant, not something the LLM is asked to respect via prompt.

(a) Model and push ACLs. Store authorization on each chunk's payload: tenant_id, visibility ('public'/'restricted'), allowed_group_ids (a list), and optionally allowed_user_ids. Create payload indexes on these fields. At query time, resolve the caller's identity into their set of group ids from the IdP/SCIM directory, then push a hard filter INTO the Qdrant search (a pre-filter), e.g. must: tenant_id == T; should: visibility == 'public' OR allowed_group_ids MATCH ANY user_groups OR allowed_user_ids contains user_id. Now ANN scoring only ranks candidates the user may see, so the top-k is both correct and complete.

(b) Filtered-ANN recall. Filtering an HNSW graph is not free: the graph is built over all vectors, so aggressively filtering during traversal can strand the search in a region with few passing neighbours and hurt recall. Qdrant mitigates this with payload-indexed 'filterable HNSW' plus a full_scan_threshold: when the filtered subset is small it falls back to an exact brute-force scan over just those points (guaranteed correct); above the threshold it uses the graph with the filter applied. That is why the filter fields must be indexed and why you tune the threshold rather than assuming a metadata filter is exact and cost-free.

(c) Consistency on membership change. Do NOT denormalize full user lists into every chunk, or a single group change forces rewriting millions of payloads (write amplification) and risks stale grants. Store slowly-changing group_ids on the documents/chunks, and resolve user->groups at query time from the authoritative directory. A revocation then takes effect on the next query with no re-indexing; keep any user->groups cache on a short TTL. When a document's OWN ACL changes, that is a cheap payload update (set_payload) with no re-embedding.

(d) Residual channel. Even with correct filtering, a response/retrieval cache keyed only on the query text will serve one principal's authorized answer to a different, less-privileged principal. Close it by keying caches on (principal or permission-set + query), and add defense-in-depth: re-check the ACL of every chunk at citation/generation time in case cached payloads are stale, and never expose filtered-result counts. (The membership-cache TTL is itself a bounded staleness window after revocation.)
